chapters.title: Chapter 6: Execution at Scale: Algos, Slicing, and Managing Impact

lessons.title: TWAP, VWAP, and POV: The Basic Execution Algorithms

children.text: Chapter 2 said spread a large order over time. Chapter 4 said cap participation at a percentage of ADV. Neither said exactly how to do that, mechanically, order by order. This lesson introduces the three basic execution algorithms every trading desk actually uses to turn those ideas into working orders.

markDefs.definition: An execution algorithm that divides an order into equal-sized slices, executed at even time intervals over a chosen window, regardless of how actual trading volume moves during that window.

children.text: , or Time-Weighted Average Price, is the simplest of the three. It splits an order into equal pieces and trades one piece every fixed interval, say every 5 minutes for 2 hours, no matter what the market is doing at that moment. It is predictable and easy to reason about, but it takes no account of the fact that trading volume is rarely spread evenly across a session.

markDefs.definition: An execution algorithm that slices an order in proportion to a historical or predicted intraday volume profile, trading more when the market typically trades more and less when it typically trades less, so the execution's own average price tracks the day's actual volume-weighted average price.

children.text: , or Volume-Weighted Average Price, instead sizes each slice according to a predicted intraday volume profile, trading more heavily during a stock's usual busy periods and lightly during its usual quiet ones. VWAP is also one of the most common institutional benchmarks in its own right, a desk asking whether an execution beat VWAP is asking a completely standard question.

markDefs.definition: An execution algorithm that continuously trades a fixed percentage of whatever volume is actually occurring in the market right now, speeding up when the market is busy and slowing down when it is quiet, rather than following any pre-set schedule.

children.text: , or Percentage of Volume, drops the pre-set schedule entirely. It watches real, live trading volume and continuously trades a fixed share of it, faster in a busy stretch, slower in a quiet one. This is the direct mechanical implementation of the participation cap from Chapter 4: set POV to 8 percent, and the algorithm enforces that cap trade by trade, in real time, rather than as a static daily plan.

cells: Simple, predictable execution when timing precision matters less
Matching a widely used institutional benchmark
Directly enforcing a participation cap like Chapter 4's 5 to 10% rule

children.text: Why Indian Intraday Volume Shape Matters for the Choice

NSE trading typically shows heavier volume in the first hour after the 9:15 AM open and the last hour before the 3:30 PM close, with a noticeably quieter stretch around midday. A TWAP order, by construction, trades the same size every interval regardless of this pattern, which means it ends up representing a larger share of the market's actual volume during the thin midday stretch than during the busy open or close, quietly raising its own impact exactly when liquidity is thinnest. VWAP and POV both lean naturally into the busier periods instead, avoiding this trap.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A trader wants to guarantee they never trade more than 8% of whatever volume is happening in the market at any given moment, automatically speeding up or slowing down with the market itself. Which execution algorithm is built for exactly this?
body.explanation: POV directly ties the trading rate to real-time market volume, enforcing a percentage-of-volume cap continuously. TWAP follows a fixed time schedule and VWAP follows a pre-built historical profile, neither reacts to what volume is actually doing right now the way POV does.

children.text: None of These Eliminate Impact, They Manage It

body.text: TWAP, VWAP, and POV are tools for distributing impact more sensibly and matching a benchmark, not ways of escaping the square-root law from Chapter 2. A badly timed order in a genuinely illiquid stock still costs real impact under any of these algorithms, the cost simply arrives in a more predictable, better-distributed way instead of all at once.

TWAP, VWAP, and POV answer the same question, when should each slice of a large order actually trade, in three different ways: by the clock, by a historical volume pattern, or by whatever the market is doing right now. Choosing between them is choosing which of those three signals you trust most for a given stock.

points: TWAP slices an order evenly across time, simple and predictable but blind to how actual volume moves during the session.
VWAP slices an order according to a historical or predicted intraday volume profile, and doubles as one of the most common institutional execution benchmarks.
POV dynamically trades a fixed percentage of real-time volume, making it the direct, mechanical implementation of Chapter 4's participation-rate cap.

NSE's typical heavier-at-open-and-close, quieter-at-midday volume pattern means a naive TWAP order can inadvertently raise its own impact during the thinnest part of the day, a trap VWAP and POV both avoid by design.
